subject: Communication
title: The Empathy Gap: Hot and Cold States
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Empathy Gap: Hot and Cold States.

hook.text: 'I'd never yell at my kids.' Then you're exhausted, hungry, and stressed — and you yell. The empathy gap strikes again.

buildup.text: George Loewenstein's research: when we're in a 'cold' state (calm), we can't predict how we'll behave in a 'hot' state.

discovery.text: This gap works both ways. In a hot state, we can't imagine being calm.

twist.text: The empathy gap also affects how we judge others. Calm people can't understand why angry people 'just don't calm down.'

climax.text: Closing the empathy gap requires remembering your own hot states — using past experience to bridge to others' current.

punchline.text: Don't judge someone's fire from the comfort of your calm.

quiz.question: What is the hot-cold empathy gap?
options: Inability to predict behavior across emotional states

details.summary: The empathy gap describes our inability to predict how emotional states will affect decisions. In a cold state, you underestimate how much pain, hunger, or anger will influence your choices. This gap causes poor planning, broken commitments, and difficulty empathizing with others in distress.
details.whyItMatters: The empathy gap explains why you make promises when calm that you cannot keep when stressed, and why you judge others' emotional decisions harshly.
takeaways: Cold states underestimate the power of hot-state emotions
The gap causes broken promises and poor self-prediction
It also reduces empathy for others in emotional states

faq.question: How can you account for the empathy gap in planning?
faq.answer: Make important decisions while imagining yourself in the relevant emotional state. Create pre-commitments while calm that constrain your hot-state behavior. Build buffer time into plans for emotional recovery. Assume you will be less rational under stress than you currently feel.

faq.question: Does the empathy gap affect how we treat others?
faq.answer: Significantly. When you feel fine, you struggle to understand why someone in pain cannot just push through. This gap drives judgmental attitudes toward people experiencing addiction, grief, or chronic pain. Recognizing the gap fosters greater compassion for others' struggles.
